chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Sidemen jam, leaders rarely do; Fletcher stayed in while Horace reported
summary: Sidemen got their jazz out in after-hours jam sessions while leaders seldom joined; Fletcher stayed home and Horace brought back reports on musicians.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: back in town, hit some of the clubs where actually there were jam sessions going on, and the guys would get a chance to play then, you know. Excuse me.
I -- but -- excuse me. But I think it's more common probably for side men to get involved in jam sessions than leaders.
I don't know why, but -- I think that's been --

Yes, that's over a period of years, it seems like that's the way it's always turned out, because a lot of times some of the side men didn't get a chance to act hip in the regular band they were playing as they would like to, so they would get those few bars of jazz out of their system after they finished, you know. But the leaders very seldom participated in it. I don't know why.
What about Fletcher? Did he participate much?

No, he didn't do too much of that. In fact, I used to bawl him out sometimes about not getting around to hear some of these other guys, you know, and usually Fletcher would stay in a lot. I would go around a lot, you know. Also the -- you know, I used to come back and report to him, and maybe this is one of the reasons why he didn't go out, because I'd come back and tell him what happened.
Because he had a good reporter, huh?
